title: Three palaces
hook: one for the rains, one for winter, one for summer; "I was delicately nurtured" (AN 3.38)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the swan, and the court that gave it to the boy who saved it. Your line was life belongs to who protects it. Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE SWAN — LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: Remember Kondañña's one raised finger, and the king who hoped his son would stay home and rule? This is where the king acts on that hope. If the boy is going to leave because he sees the world's pain, the reasoning goes, then make sure he never sees it. Wrap him in so much comfort that he never has a reason to look past the garden wall. And for years, it works. Today, in the Buddha's own words, what it was like to grow up that way.
screen: `THE PALACE.` → `A FATHER'S PLAN.` → `SO MUCH COMFORT, NO REASON TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: In one of the discourses, the Buddha looks back on his youth. He says he was raised delicately. His father had lotus ponds made just for him, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. His clothes were made of cloth from Kasi, the country around Benares. A white parasol was held over him day and night, so that cold and heat, dust and grass and dew wouldn't touch him. And he had three palaces. One for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season. During the four months of rain, he says, he stayed up in the rainy-season palace, surrounded by musicians, and never once came down. Even the servants in his father's house ate fine rice and meat, where in other houses servants got broken rice and sour gruel. No humble origin story: he grew up rich, and he says so. But then, in the same passage, the tone changes. He says: amid all that, a thought came to him. Ordinary, untaught people see someone old, and they're disgusted, forgetting that they'll grow old too. The same with sickness. The same with death. And when he saw that, he says, the pride of youth, the pride of health, the pride of being alive, all fell away from him. The three palaces kept out the rain, the heat, the cold. They couldn't keep out that thought. Comfort isn't a bad thing. But it can be a wall. And walls, sooner or later, have gates.
screen: `BLUE, RED AND WHITE LOTUS PONDS.` · `A PALACE FOR EVERY SEASON.` · `FOUR MONTHS, NEVER COMING DOWN.` · `THE PRIDE OF YOUTH FELL AWAY.` · then, large: `COMFORT CAN BE A WALL.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then look around for one comfort you forgot you had: a roof in the rain, warm water from a tap, a chair that holds you, glasses that let you see. Notice it the way the Buddha noticed his palaces, and feel a little gratitude for it. Then gently ask: is there anything it's keeping me from seeing? You don't need an answer; let the question sit beside the gratitude.
Three palaces. One for the cold, one for the heat, one for the rains: the comfort the Buddha grew up in, and the thought that got through anyway.
Your line: comfort can be a wall. A gentle line to keep beside your gratitude. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's sheltered youth as the setting for his going forth; the Sukhamala Sutta, where he describes it, is studied as a teaching on the three intoxications of youth, health and life.

fork.setup: you're a king who's been told your son will leave home if he sees the world's pain. what do you do, in the story?
options: tell him everything, and let him choose.
surround him with so much comfort he never looks past the wall.
send him to study far away.
fork.reveal: the king builds a wall of comfort: three palaces, lotus ponds, music. and for years it works, until a thought gets through.

original.note: Pali: a palace or mansion, the word used for the three seasonal palaces.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spoiled prince.
what it means: the Buddha's own account of a sheltered youth, and the thought about aging, sickness and death that the comfort couldn't keep out.
what a scholar hears: the Sukhamala Sutta (AN 3.38) and the following sutta describe the three pāsādas and the three madas, the intoxications of youth, health and life, that fall away.
recall: a steady mind that still cares

sources.ref: Sukhamala Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.38) and the following sutta (AN 3.39)

notes: The outline's hook quotes 'I was delicately nurtured'; that wording comes from a modern translation, so the script paraphrases ('raised delicately') and quotes nothing. Confirm.

AN 3.38/3.39 details paraphrased: blue, red and white lotus ponds; Kasi (Benares) cloth; white parasol against cold, heat, dust, grass and dew; three palaces; four rainy months with female musicians; servants fed rice and meat versus broken rice and sour gruel; the three intoxications. Numbering varies between editions (3.38 vs 3.39). Confirm.
The king's motive for the palaces (to prevent his son leaving) comes from later biographies, not AN 3.38. The hook frames it as 'the reasoning goes'. Confirm.
Editor review (days 20-37 pass): AN 3.38 says Kasi cloth, not 'the finest'; replaced 'the richest kid in town' (an unsourced superlative) with 'he grew up rich'.
